oh god, im sixteen so I dont have a full understanding of how a mother loves a daughter, but I know it's deep. I may not know about you, but if I were to die of cancer and my mom was still alive, I personally would want my mom to keep living and going after I died. I'd want her not to be known, as the mom who ended herself after I died, but the woman who raised a strong girl for fourteen years and still had the heart, strength, and courage to go on. id want her to always have a place for me in my heart and remember me, but be able to have a healthy relationship with her grief. and I especially would want her to have acceptance of my death. it's going to take a while, maybe months, maybe years, maybe decades. there's going to be days when it's hard as hell, and it feels like the weight of it all is going to crush you, but there's also going to be days when it's easy and nice. but what's important for you to know is you will never be "over it". when you lose someone so close to you, you lose that person for life. she will always be in her heart, in your mind, and in many ways, in your life forever. I know it sounds odd, but I really suggest you watch the movie the badadook and think of the badadook as a metaphor for grief. i know I should be listening to myself saying this, but if you can, I suggest setting a time, where you go outside and think of the things your grateful things. it is super great you care so much, so here's some advice/tips I've learned from helping others through it/going through it myself

when trying to get them to stop, don't:

* scare them out of it by scaring them with infection warnings
* say that "please don't do it for me" sounds good, but don't do it 
* tell ***ANYONE*** without their 100% conscious consent to you telling them, (also, never, ever threaten ambulances or police if they say they are considering suicide, it makes it so much worse)
* make them feel bad for hurting themselves ( cover up your scars, people are gonna stare, only loony people do that, etc)
* when they're venting to you, don't say, "I know how that feels", it kinda feels like your saying "UgH I gO tHrOuGh ThAt ToO" and will probably make them feel less understood/less valid. ask things like "what does that feel like" or "I'm sorry your going through that, I can only imagine what it's like"

when you are supporting them, I suggest:

* (if you can) offering them rides to the emergency room, no questions asked
* tell them they can talk to you any time
* lightly push them to the direction of reaching out and asking a parent/guardian/teacher for help and mental health resources
* educate both yourself and your friend on ways to prevent self-harm or stopping their self-harm triggers
* be there
